newsitem.title: MONACO: Reinsurance market mulls summer of change.
newsitem.headline: Reinsurance market mulls summer of change.

text.p: Executives from the international reinsurance industry began their annual rendezvous in Monte Carlo on Monday against a background of rapid change.

The last three months have witnessed a spree of consolidation in the industry, continued deterioration of rates, and the re-emergence of Lloyd's of London from the financial and legal quagmire which enveloped it after massive losses in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The summer of mergers and acquisitions has led to there being fewer large players. The trigger was the acquisition of National Re by General Re, followed by German insurance giant Munich Re's takeover of the second largest U.S. reinsurer American Re, and most recently the deal in which Munich's main rival Swiss Re took control of the UK's Mercantile and General Re.
These multi-million dollar deals were shadowed by similar, smaller deals involving companies such as Scor RE from France, Allstate in the U.S. and Transnational Re.
An earlier purchase of Tempest Re by Ace encouraged speculation that the consolidation trend would be echoed in the relatively young Bermudan insurance market.

The effect of these changes will be much discussed by delegates at the Monte Carlo rendezvous - an informally-structured event, now in its fortieth year, where insurers, reinsurers and brokers hold back-to-back meetings to discuss market trends and conditions as a pre-cursor to the policy renewal season.
Some attending Monte Carlo hope that putting a greater percentage of market capacity into the hands of a smaller number of players will stiffen resolve on rating and slow the downward slide.
Philip Marcell, chairman of London-based reinsurer Unionamerica outlined the problems in the run-up to the event.
"Additional capacity in London and Bermuda and elsewhere is putting a lot of pressure on both rates and terms. We are also seeing continuing consolidation of capacity."

"Unless something occurs to change this year's pattern, underwriting negotiations will be affected by the absence of major property losses in the U.S. and Europe, with minor catastrophe losses in the U.S. closely following 1995 figures."
He estimated that the price of catastrophe programmes had fallen by 30 percent in the last few years.

"If prices go too low, should a major catastrophe occur, it becomes very difficult to charge a sufficiently realistic rate to take account of the ongoing risk premium and any payback that may be necessary," said Marcell.

Reinsurers may find some hope in their bid to push rates up from the after effects of Hurricane Fran, which last week devastated the North Carolina coast in the U.S. with early insured damage estimates hitting $25 million. This will be used as a foil by reinsurers against brokers seeking further reductions because of good claims experience in the last year.
It may also help deter new capacity coming onto the market and putting further downward pressure on rates.

But as Marcell warned, the cost of business has gone up by leaps and bounds. New players in reinsurance today need to have capital of at least $50 million, and most believe $100 million is required to be taken seriously.
Operating costs are difficult to reduce to match falling rates, and the shortage of reserves cuts the potential for investment income.

One factor which may affect this year's renewal season will be the extent to which Lloyd's of London regains ground lost during the years when losses at the 300-year-old market exceeded of 8.0 billion stg.

Although Lloyd's capacity held up better than expected in recent years -- despite the scale of the problems facing the market and its backers, known as Names -- the volume of premium income written by the market has fallen.

Now that Lloyd's has pushed through its Reconstruction and Renewal plan, chairman David Rowland is encouraging underwriters to think more about future business and client relationships. Lloyd's brokers in particular will be using Rowland's success as a lever to secure new business.

Rowland is expected to make an appearance at the meeting to help the publicity wagon along. He, more than anyone, is aware that, although Lloyd's is getting the problems of the past behind it, it still has the problems of the future to overcome.
-- Gordon Mackenzie, Reuters Insurance News +377 93 50 65 00 ext 88031
